confirmed.expected: The JSDoc on the public `onExit` export (node_modules/@gtkx/runtime/dist/lifecycle.d.ts:47) says: "Registers a callback to run once when the process quits, before the native runtime is torn down." Ctrl-C and SIGTERM are how a GUI application is normally stopped, and how a supervisor stops a child, so a callback registered for "when the process quits" has to run for them. The runtime does install a process-level hook — node_modules/@gtkx/runtime/dist/exit-hook.js is exactly `import { quit } from "./lifecycle.js"; process.on("exit", quit);` — but Node only emits `exit` on a normal end of the event loop or on `process.exit()`, never for a process terminated by a signal, so that single hook cannot cover the two most common ways an app is stopped. The feature is implemented, just not wired to signals. Beyond user callbacks this also skips the shutdown work codegen itself registers: `onExit(finalize)` at node_modules/.gtkx/gi/gtksource/gtksource.js:10973 never runs on Ctrl-C.

Not a GTK limitation. The GIR docs for `g_application_run` (glib 2.88 here, /usr/share/gir-1.0/Gio-2.0.gir) describe no signal handling whatsoever, and the only `SIGTERM` mention in the whole Gio GIR is unrelated (GDBusConnection exit-on-close). GTKX deliberately never calls `g_application_run` anyway (documented at packages/runtime/src/lifecycle.ts:105-125: it "would drive its own main loop and freeze Node"). The gap is entirely inside GTKX's own Node process hook, so nothing GTK-side is being faithfully exposed.

Not API misuse. `@gtkx/runtime` is a listed public entrypoint (api.json:14), `onExit` is exported at packages/runtime/src/index.ts:10, and its only contract is the JSDoc at packages/runtime/src/lifecycle.ts:70-73 ("Registers a callback to run once when the process quits, before the native runtime is torn down"), republished verbatim at website/reference/@gtkx/runtime/variables/onExit.md. Nothing in website/guide/, website/tutorial/, or the reference scopes it away from signals.

Not a duplicate. All 30 ledger entries were read; the lifecycle neighbors are F116 (quit no-op after re-render), R106 (disconnect criticals), R107 (never exits when the last window closes), R108 (timeouts with no application mounted). None concerns signal delivery.

Not a missing feature, which is the only serious ground and the one that fails on the source. The workspace already owns both halves of this pattern and applies them everywhere else it manages a process. `packages/vitest/src/worker-preload.ts:7-8` is the in-repo template verbatim: `process.on("exit", teardown); installGracefulShutdown({ onSignal: teardown });`. `installGracefulShutdown` lives at packages/utils/src/process/install-graceful-shutdown.ts:101 and handles SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP with coalescing, force escalation and `exitCodeForSignal`; it is used by the MCP server (packages/mcp/src/server.ts:417) and the CLI dev runner (packages/cli/src/dev/runner-deps.ts:53). It is already reachable from the runtime: `@gtkx/utils` is a declared dependency in packages/runtime/package.json and packages/runtime/src/application-class.ts:1 already imports from it. `exit-hook.ts` implements only the first of the two lines.

The decisive consequence is an internal contradiction between GTKX's own two run modes for one public API. Under `gtkx dev`, packages/cli/src/dev/runner.ts:314 calls `deps.installShutdownHandlers`, so Ctrl-C reaches `onShutdownSignal` (runner.ts:152) then `finish()` then `process.exit(0)`, which emits `exit`, which runs `quit`, which runs the user's `onExit` callbacks. The identical source built with `gtkx build` and started directly has no signal handler at all, so the callbacks never run. That is a half-wired hook, not an unimplemented feature.

Extend `@gtkx/utils` to hold one shared signal registry that runs every registered `onSignal` and exits once they all settle, and register both the runtime and the worker preload through it. Cover the new path with a test beside packages/runtime/tests/lifecycle.test.ts.

rejected.title: Gio.BufferedInputStream.peek reports it copied N bytes but never writes them into the caller's array, silently dropping the peeked data
rejected.why:
Ruled out on the first listed ground (GTKX faithfully exposes a GLib/GObject-Introspection limitation) and secondarily on the fifth (what is asked for is a missing feature, not a broken path).

1. The introspection contract says `buffer` is an IN array. /usr/share/gir-1.0/Gio-2.0.gir:12496 declares `<parameter name="buffer" transfer-ownership="none">` with `<array length="2" zero-terminated="0" c:type="void*"><type name="guint8"/></array>` and NO `direction` attribute, so it defaults to `direction="in"`. Contrast g_input_stream_read at Gio-2.0.gir:74566, which does carry `direction="out" caller-allocates="1"`. GLib simply never annotated g_buffered_input_stream_peek as caller-allocates; the C function writes through the pointer it is handed, and the pointer it is handed is the binding's temporary copy. GTKX emitting `t.sizedArray(t.uint8, 3, "borrowed")` is a literal transcription of that GIR node, not a marshalling mistake.

2. The reference GI binding behaves identically on this machine. PyGObject 3.56.3 running the same operation against the same GIR prints `peek returned: 4`, `buffer after peek: [0, 0, 0, 0]`, `peek_buffer: [65, 66, 67, 68]` - byte for byte the reported GTKX output. Same annotation, same dropped data, no GTKX code involved. That also disposes of the stale-store and machine-artifact possibilities: the bughunt worktree store (regenerated 2026-08-11 19:10) reproduces, and so does a binding that reads no GTKX artifact at all.

3. GTKX's codegen already has the correct policy for genuinely caller-allocated array outs, and it is not this path. packages/codegen/src/analysis/param-capability.ts:158-160 short-circuits `direction === "in"` (which is what peek is), while lines 162-166 route caller-allocated outs to `isUnmarshalableCallerOut`, whose `hasCallerSuppliedLength` branch (line 121) makes any caller-allocated array with a length parameter unmarshalable, so the whole function is skipped. That is precisely why g_input_stream_read, graphene_matrix_to_float, graphene_rect_get_vertices and pango_break are absent from the store. peek is emitted only because GIR does not tell GTKX it is an out parameter. Verified: `read(cancellable)` in gio.d.ts:53392 is Gio.File.read; g_input_stream_read appears nowhere in the store.

4. The JSDoc the report treats as a GTKX promise is upstream text. "Peeks in the buffered input, copying `count` bytes ... into `buffer`" is the verbatim `<doc>` at Gio-2.0.gir:12480, and the `@param buffer a pointer to an allocated chunk of memory` line is the verbatim doc at 12499. GTKX adds no claim of its own; it carries the C documentation, which is accurate about C and silent about bindings.

5. GTKX's own documented convention contradicts the expectation in the report. website/guide/async-operations.md:10 states that out-parameters come back through the return value as a tuple, and website/guide/error-handling.md:8 states that no out-parameter ever appears in a JS signature. GTKX never mutates a caller-supplied JS value to deliver output. Writing back into the caller's array here would be a new, GTKX-specific inference (treat an in-annotated array as if it were caller-allocates) that no GI binding performs and that would be wrong for the many in-arrays C really only reads.

No memory-safety issue rides along: the descriptor passes `count = buffer.length` against a temporary of exactly `buffer.length` bytes, so C writes strictly in bounds of the temporary.

Not a duplicate of anything in .bughunt/findings.jsonl. F103 is a NUL-terminated marshalling of a scalar out pointer, F104 is struct-field write-back through boxed copies, F117 is a length overflow in array out decoding; none covers an in-annotated array parameter.

rejected.title: Signal handlers connected from JS never receive a signal's out parameter, so GtkSpinButton::input cannot be implemented and taking it over forces the value to 0
rejected.why:
Ruled out on the "reproduction misuses the API in a way the GTKX documentation warns about" ground, and its residual is R103 restated.

GTKX applies one uniform convention to every out parameter, across calls, promisified calls, vfuncs and signals: a pure out parameter is left out of the argument list and comes back through the return value, several outputs as a tuple led by the C return. That is stated in /home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/website/guide/subclassing.md:101 ("pure out parameters are left out of the signature and returned instead, several outputs as a tuple") and again in /home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/website/guide/async-operations.md:10-16. The generated store spells it out for this exact signal: node_modules/.gtkx/gi/gtk/gtk.d.ts:85342 declares `"input": () => [number, number]`, and the runtime implements precisely that. In packages/runtime/src/callback.ts, `partitionCallbackArgs` routes a `ref` descriptor whose `inout` is not true through `collectRefArg`, which deliberately pushes nothing into `inputs` and instead registers an `OutParam`; `runCallback` then feeds the handler's return through `splitTupleResult` and `writeOutParams`, which writes `toNative(descriptor.innerDescriptor, outValue)` back into the pointer. Zero handler arguments for `::input` is the designed contract, not a dropped parameter.

The report's central claim, "there is no combination that sets the value the handler computed", is false. Verified 
under the headless compositor with /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/marshal-r1/verify-contract.mjs:
  [1, 42] with text "12"   -> 42
  [1, 42] with text "junk" -> 42
  [1, 7.5] with text "junk"-> 7.5
  [0, 42] with text "12"   -> 12  (returning 0/FALSE correctly falls through to the default g_strtod parser)
  handler arg count 0, returning [1, 99] -> value 99
So custom spin-button parsing, the exact use the report says is impossible, works, including for text the default parser cannot handle. GTK4's documented contract is satisfied.

The `::insert-text` half is false too. `t.ref(t.int32, true)` is inout, so `collectRefArg` pushes the current value into `inputs` and registers the write-back; the typing is `(text, length, position) => number`. Verified with verify-position2.mjs that the returned position reaches C: a first handler returning 77 was observed as `position === 77` by a second handler on the same emission. The "update *position" contract is honoured through the return value.

The GIR backs GTKX's descriptors exactly (/usr/share/gir-1.0/Gtk-4.0.gir:136931-136956): return `gint`, `new_value` `direction="out" caller-allocates="0"` -> `t.int32` and `t.ref(t.float64)`.

What the repro actually did was write plain .mjs and return a bare `1`, a bare `true`, or `[true, 42]`, none of which is the declared `[number, number]`. A bare `1` leaves `outValues` empty, so `toNative(float64, undefined)` writes 0 while the handler reports success; `[true, 42]` puts a boolean where int32 is declared, so the return reads 0/FALSE and GTK falls through to its own parser. Both are the numeric codecs coercing a wrong-typed or absent value to 0, which is ledger entry R103, already rejected. The one thing that is genuinely permissive is the escape-hatch overload `connect(signal: string, handler: (...args: any[]) => any, ...)` sitting beside the typed one at gtk.d.ts:85735, which is why tsc does not reject the mistyped handler; that overload exists for runtime-registered and detail-suffixed signal names, and missing strictness there is not the wrong-result defect being reported.

rejected.title: Gdk.Texture.download and TextureDownloader.downloadInto expose a C output buffer as a plain `number`, so every call a user can type either segfaults or trips a Gdk-CRITICAL
rejected.why:
Ruled out on three of the listed grounds.

(1) The central factual claim is false. The report asserts "there is no correct argument to pass" and "Nothing in the public surface produces a valid pointer number, so no call succeeds". The same generated store exposes `GLib.malloc(nBytes): number | null`, `malloc0`, `malloc0N`, `mallocN`, `tryMalloc*`, `memdup2`, `sliceAlloc*` (node_modules/.gtkx/gi/glib/glib.d.ts:23497, 23508, 23521, 23534, 23595, 23608, 24550, 26548) and consumers such as `GLib.free` and `GVariant.getData(): number | null` (glib.d.ts:17386) - 215 declarations in the GLib store alone use this pointer-as-`number` convention. I verified the call succeeds and is correct end to end (/home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/marshal-r1/verify-texture-download-checksum.mjs): with `const data = GLib.malloc0(stride * height); texture.download(data, stride);` the process does not crash, and a SHA1 computed over the filled buffer via `g_compute_checksum_for_data` equals the SHA1 of the pixels returned by the working `Gdk.TextureDownloader.downloadBytes()` path - both `0f23198969cc3da5b64f4a67b4c96955b8ec441d`, stride 596. The pointer round-trips intact (0x1e76f0b0). The repro passes the integer literal `1` as a pointer, which is API misuse of the same class already rejected as R102/R103: an invalid pointer segfaults in C too, and `0` trips GTK's own `g_return_if_fail (data != NULL)` precondition, which the observed output quotes verbatim as `gdk_texture_download: assertion 'data != NULL' failed`.

(2) GTKX faithfully exposes the GTK4 annotation. In /usr/share/gir-1.0/Gdk-4.0.gir:33746 the parameter is `<parameter name="data" transfer-ownership="none"><array zero-terminated="0" c:type="guchar*"><type name="guint8" c:type="guchar"/></array></parameter>` - direction defaults to `in`, there is no `length=`, no `fixed-size`, no `(out caller-allocates)`. `gdk_texture_downloader_download_into` (Gdk-4.0.gir:34233) is annotated identically. The buffer size is stride x height, which no binding can derive from the introspection data; only semantic knowledge of the function yields it. The GTK documentation for the parameter says exactly "pointer to enough memory to be filled with the downloaded data", and GTKX's generated JSDoc reproduces that sentence. `packages/codegen/src/gir/type-id.ts:95` (`hasUnknownArrayLength`), `packages/codegen/src/analysis/ts-type.ts:104` (renders `number`) and `packages/codegen/src/analysis/descriptor-render.ts:716` (renders `t.uint64`) are a deliberate, coherent model of "a C array whose length the GIR does not describe is a raw pointer", not an accident.

(3) The report's premise that this escaped an existing drop rule is wrong. `hasUnmarshalableParam` skips a callable only through `isUnmarshalableCallParam` (packages/codegen/src/analysis/param-capability.ts:149), which short-circuits at line 158 on `direction === "in"`; `g_input_stream_read` and `graphene_matrix_to_float` are dropped because their buffers are `(out caller-allocates)` with a caller-supplied length, via `isUnmarshalableCallerOut` -> `hasCallerSuppliedLength` (param-capability.ts:111-126). `data` here is an `in` parameter per the GIR, so no drop rule applies to it and none is being bypassed. Turning it into a copied-back JS byte array would require a hand-written per-function override encoding sizing information the GIR does not state - a new capability, not the repair of a broken one.

Not a duplicate of any ledger entry (F103 is a NUL-terminated out-array codec defect in `GLib.utf8Validate`; F105 is opaque boxed constructors that unconditionally throw and have no working call at all, unlike this method).

rejected.title: A gunichar property installed by a registered subclass rejects the one-character string its own paramSpecUnichar default is declared to take, and reads that default back as a codepoint number
rejected.why:
Ruled out on ground 1: the GLib C API documentation says this is the correct behavior, and the report's premise about GTKX's own representation is false.

1. GLib documents the guint. g_param_spec_unichar's own doc comment, carried verbatim in /usr/share/gir-1.0/GObject-2.0.gir, reads: "Creates a new #GParamSpecUnichar instance specifying a %G_TYPE_UINT property. #GValue structures for this property can be accessed with g_value_set_uint() and g_value_get_uint()." The property a unichar ParamSpec installs holds a guint. packages/runtime/src/properties.ts:86 checkFor derives the accessor from getParamValueType(handle), the ParamSpec's value_type, which GLib sets to G_TYPE_UINT here; readStored (line 218) seeds the accessor from g_param_spec_get_default_value, a G_TYPE_UINT GValue. Reading 120 and refusing "y" with "the property holds values of type 'guint'" is GTKX reporting the GValue type GLib itself installed. Any C consumer doing g_object_get on that property gets a guint.

2. GTKX did not settle on a one-character string for gunichar properties. Every gunichar-backed GObject property in the generated store is a uint32 number, not a string: node_modules/.gtkx/gi/gtk/gtk.js line 99067 maps "invisibleChar": ["invisible-char", t.uint32]; the construct props type it invisibleChar?: number (gtk.d.ts:40404); the JSX store types it number and records its default as the number 42 (jsx/metadata.js:3335). A grep for t.unichar across every property map in the whole generated store returns nothing. Gtk.Entry's get invisibleChar(): string is not the property path at all: gtk.js:32698 delegates to this.getInvisibleChar()/this.setInvisibleChar(), the C method pair. GIR types the property <type name="guint"/> and types the method argument gunichar, and GTKX maps each faithfully: gunichar function arguments and returns get t.unichar (a one-character string or a codepoint number, per packages/native/src/ffi/codec/unichar.rs), guint properties get t.uint32. g_param_spec_unichar is exactly the place where GLib bridges the two, taking a gunichar argument to describe a G_TYPE_UINT property; the asymmetry originates in GLib, not GTKX.

3. The property is not broken, only numeric. Probed at /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/subclass-r1/probes2/unichar-check.ts: paramSpecUnichar(..., 120, ...) reads back 120; writing 0x1D11E (the astral character the report used) reads back 119070; a construct-time { glyph: 121 } reads back 121; paramSpecUint behaves identically. The subclass property round-trips fully in the guint representation GLib prescribes, which is also the representation the rest of the generated property surface uses. 120 is the codepoint of "x", so the default is preserved, not corrupted.

4. No GTKX API claims otherwise. website/guide/subclassing.md documents that a registerClass property's accessors "validate against the ParamSpec" and that the member is typed by the subclasser's own declare. The reproduction's declare glyph: string is its own assertion, not a GTKX typing; declare glyph: number is the declaration that matches the G_TYPE_UINT property GLib installed.

Not a duplicate: no entry in .bughunt/findings.jsonl covers ParamSpec value types or gunichar. Not machine-specific: it reproduces from the installed system GIR and the generated store, which agree with each other.

rejected.title: userEvent.keyboard silently drops every printable character while still applying the named keys in the same sequence, so a mixed sequence deletes text that was never inserted
rejected.why:
Ruled out on two of the listed grounds: (a) GTK4 itself cannot insert text from a synthesized key, and (b) what is missing is a feature `keyboard` never claimed, not a broken path. Evidence, all from probes I ran in /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/testkit-r1/tests/judge-keyboard-printable.test.tsx (3/3 pass):

1. The character is not dropped. `keyboard(entry, "!")` reaches the target's `Gtk.EventControllerKey` as `key-pressed(33, 0, 0)` followed by `key-released`, and 33 is exactly `Gdk.KEY_exclam`. `parseCharAt` (packages/testing/src/user-event/keyboard.ts:96) maps the code point to the correct keyval and `applyKeyAction` (:313) emits both halves. The dispatch happens; only the input-method commit does not.

2. GTK4 does not turn that emission into text either. Probe 2 attaches a plain `Gtk.EventControllerKey` to the `GtkText` delegate of a `GtkEntry` with zero GTKX helper code and emits `key-pressed`/`key-released` with `Gdk.KEY_exclam`; the entry still reads "hello". Insertion in GTK4 happens inside `gtk_event_controller_key_handle_event`, which runs the key through `gtk_im_context_filter_keypress` on a GdkEvent delivered by the display; the `key-pressed` signal is documented in /usr/share/gir-1.0/Gtk-4.0.gir only as "Emitted whenever a key is pressed", downstream of that commit, and `gtk_event_controller_key_forward` is documented as forwarding "the current event", which a synthesized emission does not have. GTK4 offers no way to manufacture one: `GdkKeyEvent` exposes only accessors (`gdk_key_event_get_keyval` and friends, no constructor), and GTK3's `gtk_test_widget_send_key` is gone (`gtk_test_*` in the GIR is accessibility assertions plus `gtk_test_init`/`wait_for_draw`). No signal-level harness can produce an IM commit, so GTKX is exposing a GTK4 boundary, not a defect.

3. The "half-applied sequence" is uniform GTK behavior, not a GTKX special case. Probe 3 enumerates the shortcut triggers on the entry's `GtkText` delegate: `BackSpace`, `Delete`, `Return`, `<Control>a`, `<Control>z`, `Home`, `End` and the rest of GtkText's own class binding set, and no `exclam` trigger. `didDispatchDelegateShortcuts` (keyboard.ts:284) applies one rule to every key: dispatch whatever GTK bound to it. Backspace acts because GTK bound it; `!` does nothing because GTK bound nothing to it, which is what an application with no input method does. The report's premise that Backspace is honored while `!` is "ignored" describes GTK's binding set, not a GTKX inconsistency.

4. The documented contract is shortcut dispatch, and printable code points exist to serve it. The reference (website/reference/@gtkx/testing/type-aliases/UserEvent.md:142) says "Sends a key sequence, dispatching matching shortcuts and tracking held modifiers across calls", while `type` is separately documented as "Focuses an editable widget, applies any initial selection, and inserts the text at the cursor". `parseCharAt` is required for the documented example `userEvent.keyboard(entry, "{Control>}a{/Control}")` (website/guide/testing.md:90) and for delivering letter keys to key controllers, which the suite asserts at packages/e2e/tests/elements/widget.test.tsx:137 and :666 (`userEvent.keyboard(button, "a")` expecting `onKeyPressed`). Every documented example inserts characters with `type` and uses `keyboard` for named keys and modifiers, including the two-step form the report cites at website/tutorial/testing.md:116-118. Insertion from a printable key would be new behavior layered on top of the key dispatch, i.e. a feature.

Not a duplicate: F111 covers ancestor delivery of key events (and this worktree already carries `didDispatchShortcutsOnAncestors`), F110 covers `type`/`paste` over a selection, R105 covers modifiers reaching `click`. None cover printable-key text insertion.

rejected.title: Every element's generated props type accepts `children`, so JSX for an element that has no children slot typechecks and then kills the app on startup
rejected.why: Ruled out on three of the listed grounds. (1) The report's central premise is factually wrong. It claims these elements "have no children slot and the runtime refuses [children] unconditionally", so `children?: ReactNode` is declared on elements that "can never take one". Every `GtkWidget` does have a working default children slot: /home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/react/src/element-behaviors.ts:62-71 registers `slot<Gtk.Widget, Gtk.Popover>("children", "GtkPopover", { attach: (parent, popover) => popover.setParent(parent), detach: ... })` on `GtkWidget`, and subtypes inherit it. The attach is selective, not unconditional: `slotAttach` in packages/react/src/reconciler/behaviors.ts:65 returns undefined unless `isMatch(child)` holds, and `runAttach` (packages/react/src/reconciler/placement.ts:121) only throws after no behavior claimed the child. I verified this against the same six elements the report names, in the hunter's own app with the same @gtkx/*@1.0.0 packages: /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/higapp-r1b/tests/children-popover.test.tsx renders `<GtkPopover>` as the child of AdwHeaderBar, AdwBanner, AdwTabBar, AdwSpinner, GtkProgressBar and GtkSeparator and none produces the "cannot be a child of" error, and /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/higapp-r1b/tests/children-popover-parent.test.tsx asserts `popover.getParent()` is the `GtkSeparator` and the `AdwHeaderBar` respectively (2/2 pass). So `ChildrenProps` on `GtkWidgetProps` (packages/react/src/prop-types.ts:104) is a correct declaration, and its doc "Elements attached to the element's default child slot" describes exactly the popover slot. There is no element in the set the report proposes to strip `children` from. (2) The asked-for behavior is not expressible in TypeScript, so it is a missing capability of the React JSX type model rather than a broken GTKX declaration. React's own types define `interface Element extends React.ReactElement<any, any> {}` (higapp-r1b/node_modules/@types/react/index.d.ts:4153), so a JSX expression carries no element identity at all. I proved the consequence directly: /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/higapp-r1b/repro/children-type/narrowing-probe.tsx declares the narrowest possible children type, `ReactElement<{ popoverBrand: "GtkPopover" }>`, assigns `<GtkButton label="New" />` to it, and `tsc --strict` exits 0. Whatever GTKX declared for `children`, `<AdwHeaderBar><GtkButton/></AdwHeaderBar>` would still typecheck. (3) The reproduction uses a form GTK4 and the GTKX documentation both direct away from. GtkHeaderBar has no child property: children are packed with `gtk_header_bar_pack_start()` / `gtk_header_bar_pack_end()`, which GTKX surfaces as the `start` and `end` props (packages/react/src/element-config.ts:37-39, behaviors at element-behaviors.ts:34-56). website/tutorial/your-first-window.md:138 states the rule ("some props are container slots rather than values. A widget with more than one place to put a child exposes each place as its own prop"), and the tutorial teaches the correct form at actions-menus-shortcuts.md:132 (`end={<MainMenu />}`), the-task-editor.md:386 and trash-and-toasts.md:369 (`start={...}`). The runtime error the repro hits names that fix in its first clause. Not a duplicate of anything in .bughunt/findings.jsonl; F105 is the nearest in spirit (typechecks then throws) but concerns opaque boxed record constructors in the gi store, a different surface and a different cause.

rejected.title: The async guide's documented catch for a cancelled GTK4 dialog does not match Gtk.AlertDialog.choose, which rejects in the Gio.IOErrorEnum domain
rejected.why:
The observed behavior is an upstream GTK4 bug that GTKX marshals faithfully, and the GTKX guide sentence the report calls wrong is an accurate restatement of GTK's own documented contract.

1. GTK's documentation says the guide's rule is correct, not the observed behavior. /usr/share/gir-1.0/Gtk-4.0.gir line 43638 documents GTK_DIALOG_ERROR_CANCELLED as "The async function call was cancelled via its `GCancellable`" (from gtk/gtkdialogerror.h:42), against GTK_DIALOG_ERROR_DISMISSED as "The operation was cancelled by the user (via a Cancel or Close button)". website/guide/async-operations.md:48 says exactly that: GTK4 dialogs reject with CANCELLED in Gtk.DialogError. The guide agrees with the upstream contract; upstream's AlertDialog implementation is what violates it.

2. GTK's source shows it intends GTK_DIALOG_ERROR_CANCELLED and loses it to a GTask default. In upstream gtk/gtkalertdialog.c, response_cb executes `g_task_return_new_error (task, GTK_DIALOG_ERROR, GTK_DIALOG_ERROR_CANCELLED, "Cancelled by application")` on the cancelled path, but gtk_alert_dialog_choose never calls `g_task_set_check_cancellable (task, FALSE)` (the string does not appear in the file). With the check left at its TRUE default, g_task_propagate_int in gtk_alert_dialog_choose_finish discards GTK's own error and substitutes G_IO_ERROR_CANCELLED. gtk/gtkfiledialog.c calls `g_task_set_check_cancellable (task, FALSE)` in all eight of its async entry points, which is precisely why FileDialog reports gtk-dialog-error-quark/1 and AlertDialog does not. The message strings confirm the override: the repro sees GTask's stock "Operation was cancelled" for AlertDialog versus GTK's own "Cancelled by application" for FileDialog. This is a one-line upstream omission in GTK, not a GTKX behavior.

3. I confirmed it is not GTKX code and not this machine. The report's own C control, recompiled and rerun here against GTK 4.22.4 under the same headless compositor with zero GTKX in the process, prints `AlertDialog cancelled-during: CALLBACK error domain=g-io-error-quark code=19 msg=Operation was cancelled`. The GTKX repro (10/10) reproduces the identical domain and code, so GTKX changes nothing.

4. The GTKX code path is a faithful pass-through. packages/runtime/src/promisify.ts `settle` (line 28) simply rejects with whatever the generated finish function throws, and packages/runtime/src/error.ts `checkError` (line 25) wraps the raw GError, while `createErrorDomain` (line 47) backs instanceof on the GError's domain quark alone. There is no domain remapping, no cancellation special case, nothing GTKX could be getting wrong here.

5. Not a duplicate: nothing in /home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/.bughunt/findings.jsonl covers dialog error domains or the async guide.

Amending the guide to enshrine the exception would document an upstream defect that disappears the moment GTK adds the missing call, leaving the guide wrong in the other direction. The correct destination for this report is the GTK issue tracker.

rejected.title: useBindSetting's `property` is an unvalidated plain string, so a misspelling type-checks and then either aborts the process on a GLib critical or silently binds nothing
rejected.why:
Ruled out on two of the listed grounds: faithful exposure of GLib behavior, plus a missing feature rather than a broken one.

1. GLib defines the runtime half. `/usr/share/gir-1.0/Gio-2.0.gir` declares `g_settings_bind(settings, key, object, property, flags)` with `property` as `utf8 / const gchar*`, and gsettings.c reports a nonexistent property through `g_critical("g_settings_bind: no property '%s' on class '%s'")`. That is a programmer-error diagnostic, identical in C, gjs, PyGObject and Vala. `useBindSetting` passes the string through verbatim (packages/react/src/hooks/use-bind-setting.ts:44), so the critical, the absent binding, and the SIGABRT under `G_DEBUG=fatal-criticals` are GLib doing what GLib documents. `@gtkx/vitest` sets that variable on purpose so criticals fail tests, which makes exit 134 the designed outcome, not a defect.

2. Plain-string property names are the norm across the GTKX surface, not an outlier in this hook. The generated store types them exactly as GIR does: `node_modules/.gtkx/gi/gio/gio.d.ts:28084` has `bind(key: string, object: GObject.Object, property: string, flags: SettingsBindFlags): void`, and `node_modules/.gtkx/gi/gobject/gobject.d.ts:2581` has `bindProperty(sourceProperty: string, target: Object, targetProperty: string, flags: BindingFlags): Binding`. `useBindSetting`'s `property: string` matches the method it wraps. The narrowing on `useProperty` (`PropertyName<T>` from `T["__properties__"]`) and `useSignal` (`SignalName<T>` from `T["__signals__"]`) is an extra layer GTKX applies where the hook is already generic over the object type; `UseBindSettingOptions` is generic only over the schema keys (`K`), and its `object` is typed `RefProp<GObject.Object>`, so there is no `T` to narrow against. Extending that narrowing to a third hook is an enhancement to an API that never claimed the guarantee: the JSDoc says only "camelCase name of the property to keep in sync with the key", and the hook's documented job (bind a key to a property) works correctly for every valid input.
